title: Drawing, Naming & Representing Drug Molecules
summary: How chemists encode molecules for papers, databases and computers.

lessons.title: IUPAC names vs drug (INN) names & stems

levels.kid:
Every medicine has more than one name, like a person with a full name, a nickname and a team jersey name.

The **chemical name** is super long. It describes every piece of the molecule, like a map. Chemists use it.

The **generic name** is shorter, and every country uses the same one. Doctors use it. Ibuprofen is a generic name.

The **brand name** is what a company calls its product, like a sneaker brand.

Here is a cool trick: generic names have family endings. Medicines ending in "-olol" slow the heart, and ones ending in "-cillin" are cousins of penicillin. So the ending tells you which family the medicine belongs to!
levels.hs:
A drug usually has three kinds of names.

**Chemical (IUPAC) name.** A systematic name built by rules from the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry. It fully describes the structure. Ibuprofen's is 2-[4-(2-methylpropyl)phenyl]propanoic acid. Precise, but long.

**Generic name (INN).** The International Nonproprietary Name, chosen by the World Health Organization, is the official worldwide name: ibuprofen, atorvastatin, metoprolol. In the US the matching system is USAN; a few drugs differ by country (paracetamol is the INN, acetaminophen the US name).

**Brand name.** A trademark owned by a company, and the same drug can have many brands in different countries.

The smartest part of generic names is the **stem**, a shared syllable that signals the drug's class:

- **-olol**: β-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol)
- **-pril**: ACE inhibitors (lisinopril)
- **-sartan**: angiotensin II receptor blockers (losartan)
- **-statin**: cholesterol-lowering HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors
- **-prazole**: proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole)
- **-tinib**: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib)
- **-mab**: monoclonal antibodies (adalimumab)
- **-vir**: antivirals (acyclovir)
- **-cillin** / **cef-**: penicillins / cephalosporins

Know the stem and you can guess what an unfamiliar drug does.
levels.college:
**IUPAC nomenclature** derives a unique systematic name from the structure: identify the parent chain or ring, the principal characteristic group (suffix: -oic acid, -amide, -ol), substituents as prefixes in alphabetical order with locants, and stereodescriptors (R/S, E/Z). Paracetamol is N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide; aspirin is 2-(acetyloxy)benzoic acid. Because IUPAC rules allow choices, databases also rely on registry numbers (CAS RN) and structure-based identifiers.

**INNs** have been assigned by the WHO since 1950 (the first list was published in 1953). National systems (USAN in the US, BAN in the UK) are now largely harmonized with INNs. An INN names the active moiety; salts and esters are named separately (sertraline hydrochloride, but the INN is sertraline).

INNs are built from **stems** that indicate pharmacological or chemical relationship. The stem goes at the end or, less often, at the start or middle. Important ones:

- -olol (β-adrenergic antagonists), -pril (ACE inhibitors), -sartan (AT1 antagonists), -dipine (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers)
- -statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors), -gliptin (DPP-4 inhibitors), -gliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitors)
- -tidine (H2 antagonists), -prazole (proton pump inhibitors), -setron (5-HT3 antagonists), -triptan (5-HT1B/1D agonists)
- -floxacin (fluoroquinolones), -conazole (azole antifungals), -vir (antivirals, with sub-stems such as -navir for HIV protease inhibitors)
- -tinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitors), -parib (PARP inhibitors), -mab (monoclonal antibodies), -cept (receptor–Fc fusion proteins)

Stereochemistry often appears in names: es- or lev(o)- for single enantiomers (esomeprazole is S-omeprazole; levocetirizine is the R-enantiomer of cetirizine), dex- for dextrorotatory forms. Note that "levo" refers to optical rotation, not the R/S label.
levels.phd:
Drug nomenclature is a layered information system, and each layer encodes something different.

**Systematic names** encode constitution and configuration but are not unique in practice: IUPAC permits several valid names, and complex natural products or biologics are unwieldy. Hence structure-derived identifiers (InChI) and registries (CAS RN, UNII from the FDA's Global Substance Registration System) carry the identity burden in regulatory and database contexts.

**INN stems** encode a pharmacological or structural relationship, decided by the WHO INN Expert Group. Stems are not always mechanistic: -olol was assigned by structure (aryloxypropanolamine β-antagonists), which is why some -olol drugs have additional actions (labetalol and carvedilol also block α1). Stems can also be subdivided: -tinib for tyrosine kinase inhibitors versus -rafenib for RAF inhibitors and -ciclib for cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors. Pre-stem syllables are deliberately arbitrary and chosen to avoid confusion with existing names.

**Biologic naming** has been revised repeatedly. Monoclonal antibodies used -mab with substem infixes for target class (-li- for immunomodulating, -tu- for tumour, later revised) and source (-xi- chimeric, -zu- humanized, -u- human, -o- mouse), giving names such as infliximab and trastuzumab. In 2017 the source infix was dropped for new names because humanization had become a continuum, and in 2021 the WHO announced replacement of -mab with four new suffixes for new antibodies: -tug (unmodified immunoglobulins), -bart (artificial, engineered antibodies), -mig (multispecific) and -ment (fragments). In the US, biologics also carry a four-letter suffix that distinguishes products (for example infliximab-dyyb for a biosimilar).

**Enantiomer naming** reflects the chiral-switch era: when a racemate's single enantiomer is developed separately (escitalopram, esomeprazole, levocetirizine, dexlansoprazole), the INN adds a prefix. The prefixes es-/ar- relate to S/R configuration while lev-/dex- relate to optical rotation sign, which is not predictable from R/S.
levels.expert:
For a practising medicinal chemist or physician, names are a tool and a hazard.

**Reading a new drug name.** A chemist who sees "-ciclib" thinks CDK4/6 inhibitor; "-lisib", PI3K inhibitor; "-degib", Hedgehog (Smoothened) pathway; "-rafenib", RAF; "-tide", peptide; "-siran", small interfering RNA; "-rsen", antisense oligonucleotide; "-gene", gene therapy. A clinician uses the same stems to spot class effects and duplicate therapy, for example two -prazoles or an -olol plus another β-blocker.

**Stem pitfalls.** Stems signal relationship, not identical behaviour. Within -olol, selectivity (metoprolol β1-selective, propranolol non-selective), intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and lipophilicity (which affects CNS side effects) vary. Some important drugs predate stems and have idiosyncratic names. Fluoroquinolones share -floxacin but not identical spectrum or QT risk.

**Safety.** Look-alike, sound-alike names cause medication errors (hydroxyzine/hydralazine, or the brands Celebrex and Celexa). Regulators screen new names against existing ones, and hospitals use "tall man" lettering (hydrOXYzine, hydrALAZINE) to reduce errors.

**Salts and labels.** Labels state the salt, and product strength may refer to the salt or the free base depending on the jurisdiction and product, a detail that matters when comparing formulations. The chemist chooses the salt (hydrochloride, mesylate, besylate, tosylate) for solubility, stability and crystallinity; imatinib is marketed as the mesylate, amlodipine commonly as the besylate.

**Structure search over name search.** In a project, never rely on a name or a code number to identify a compound. Development codes change hands, papers mislabel structures, and stereochemistry is often omitted. Register compounds by structure (with stereochemistry and salt form recorded separately) and search databases by structure or InChIKey.

A senior chemist's habit: when reading a paper, draw the structure from the systematic name or SMILES yourself and check that it matches the figure.

keyPoints: Drugs have a systematic (IUPAC) name, a generic name (INN, set by WHO) and brand names.
INN stems signal the drug class: -olol, -pril, -sartan, -statin, -prazole, -tinib, -mab, -vir.
The INN names the active moiety; the salt (e.g. hydrochloride) is named separately.
Single-enantiomer drugs often get prefixes such as es- (esomeprazole) or lev(o)- (levocetirizine).
Antibody names moved from -mab to -tug, -bart, -mig and -ment for new antibodies (WHO, 2021).

lessons.title: SMILES, InChI & chemical databases

levels.kid:
How do you tell a computer what a molecule looks like? You can't just show it a drawing. So chemists invented a secret code made of letters!

It is called **SMILES**. Each letter is an atom: C is carbon, O is oxygen, N is nitrogen. Letters next to each other are holding hands.

So "CCO" means carbon holding carbon holding oxygen. That is alcohol, the kind in hand sanitizer!

There is also a longer code called **InChI** that gives every molecule one special ID, like a fingerprint.

Chemists put millions of these codes into giant online libraries, so anyone can search for a molecule in seconds.
levels.hs:
Computers need molecules as text, so chemists invented line notations.

**SMILES** (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System) writes a molecule as a string:

- Atoms are element symbols; hydrogens are usually left out (they are implied).
- Neighbouring atoms are bonded: CCO is ethanol.
- = is a double bond, # is a triple bond: CC(=O)O is acetic acid.
- Parentheses show branches: CC(C)C is isobutane.
- Numbers open and close rings, and lowercase letters mean aromatic atoms: c1ccccc1 is benzene, c1ccncc1 is pyridine.
- Stereochemistry uses @ and @@ for chiral centres and / and \ for double-bond geometry.

Aspirin is CC(=O)Oc1ccccc1C(=O)O. One molecule can be written as many valid SMILES, so software produces a **canonical SMILES**, one standard version.

**InChI** (International Chemical Identifier), created by IUPAC, gives each structure a single standard string organised in layers (formula, connections, hydrogens, charge, stereochemistry). Its short hashed form, the **InChIKey**, is 27 characters and works well for web searches.

Major free databases: **PubChem** (over 100 million compounds), **ChEMBL** (bioactivity data from papers), **DrugBank** (drugs and their targets), and the **PDB** (3D structures of proteins, often with drugs bound).
levels.college:
**SMILES** (Weininger, 1988) encodes the molecular graph as a depth-first traversal. Rules: organic-subset atoms (B, C, N, O, P, S, F, Cl, Br, I) may be written bare with implicit hydrogens; anything else, or atoms with explicit charge, isotope or unusual valence, goes in brackets ([NH4+], [O-], [13C]). Bonds: single (implicit or -), double =, triple #, aromatic (implied between lowercase atoms). Branches go in parentheses; ring closures use matching digits (c1ccccc1). Isomeric SMILES adds @/@@ for tetrahedral centres (looking from the first neighbour, the remaining neighbours run anticlockwise for @ and clockwise for @@) and / \ for E/Z. L-alanine is C[C@@H](C(=O)O)N.

Because many SMILES describe the same molecule, toolkits generate **canonical SMILES**, but canonicalization is toolkit-specific: RDKit, OpenEye and ChemAxon produce different canonical strings for the same molecule. **SMARTS** extends SMILES into a query language for substructure searching (for example, [CX3](=O)[OX2H1] matches a carboxylic acid).

**InChI** (IUPAC/InChI Trust, 2005) is canonical by design and toolkit-independent. A Standard InChI has layers: formula, connectivity (/c), hydrogens (/h), charge and protonation (/q, /p), stereo (/b, /t, /m, /s) and isotopes. Mobile hydrogens are normalized, so many tautomers share one InChI. The **InChIKey** is a 27-character SHA-256-based hash: a 14-character connectivity block, a hyphen, a 10-character block (eight hash characters for stereo and the other layers, then a standard flag and a version letter), a hyphen, and one protonation character. Ethanol's InChIKey is LFQSCWFLJHTTHZ-UHFFFAOYSA-N. The hash cannot be converted back into a structure.

**Molfile/SDF** formats store explicit atom and bond tables with 2D or 3D coordinates and are the usual exchange format.

Databases: PubChem (NIH; compounds, substances and bioassays), ChEMBL (EMBL-EBI; curated bioactivities), DrugBank, BindingDB, ZINC (purchasable compounds for virtual screening), PDB (macromolecular structures) and the CSD (small-molecule crystal structures).
levels.phd:
Line notations are lossy representations of a chemical graph, and the choice of what to lose has consequences.

SMILES uses a valence model with implicit hydrogens and an aromaticity model. Aromaticity perception differs across toolkits (Daylight, RDKit, OpenEye), so the same lowercase SMILES may be parsed or kekulized differently, and some heteroaromatic SMILES are rejected by one toolkit and accepted by another. Canonicalization requires solving graph symmetry (Morgan-type extended connectivity ranking plus tie-breaking); errors in symmetry handling historically produced different "canonical" strings for identical molecules.

Newer representations address specific weaknesses. **SELFIES** (2020) is a grammar in which every string decodes to a valid molecule, which is useful for generative models that otherwise produce invalid SMILES. **DeepSMILES** simplifies ring and branch syntax. For biologics, **HELM** represents peptides, oligonucleotides and conjugates with monomer libraries, because atom-level SMILES of an antibody is impractical.

InChI's design choices are equally consequential. Standard InChI normalizes mobile hydrogens, so many tautomers collapse to one identifier, convenient for deduplication but a problem when tautomers differ biologically. Keto–enol and ring–chain tautomerism are not covered by standard rules. The connectivity layer disconnects metals, which affects organometallics and metal complexes such as cisplatin. Stereo is encoded only when defined; an unspecified centre and a racemate can be indistinguishable unless flags are used.

InChIKey collisions are theoretically possible but extremely rare in practice for the first block. The more practical issue is that the hash is one-way, so lookup depends on a resolver database.

Database curation is a research problem in itself. Studies of public bioactivity sets report substantial rates of structure errors, inconsistent stereochemistry and duplicated measurements with different units. Standardization pipelines (salt stripping, neutralization, tautomer canonicalization, stereo checks), such as the ChEMBL structure pipeline, are essential before modelling. Using raw database exports without them propagates errors into QSAR and machine-learning models.
levels.expert:
In an industrial or academic lab, these tools are part of everyday workflow, and mistakes are costly.

**Registration.** Every new compound is registered in a corporate database by structure, with salt, stereochemical descriptors (racemic, relative, absolute, unknown), batch and purity recorded separately. A good registration system flags duplicates by canonical structure and catches errors like a drawn enantiomer that was actually made as a racemate.

**Searching.** Exact searches use canonical SMILES or InChIKey; similarity searches use fingerprints; substructure searches use SMARTS. Before starting synthesis on a new idea, chemists search SciFinder (CAS) or Reaxys for prior art and known routes, and PubChem or ChEMBL for known activity. A quick InChIKey web search often finds every database entry and paper for a compound in seconds.

**Data hygiene.** When pulling activity data from ChEMBL, check assay type (binding versus functional), units, species, and whether values are censored (">10 µM"). Merge data only from comparable assays. Strip salts and standardize tautomers and charges before computing descriptors.

**SMILES pitfalls.** Missing stereochemistry silently turns a single enantiomer into an undefined structure. Explicit-hydrogen and charge differences ([nH] in pyrroles and imidazoles) cause parsing failures. Copying SMILES from a PDF can corrupt characters. Always re-render a SMILES as a drawing and look at it before using it.

**Structural biology resources.** The PDB is invaluable but not infallible: ligand geometry and placement in older or low-resolution structures can be poorly supported by the electron density. Check resolution, ligand B-factors and the density map (via validation reports) before designing around a pose.

**Machine learning.** Models built on SMILES strings or graphs inherit every curation error in the training data. Teams increasingly use rigorous splits (scaffold or time splits) to avoid optimistic performance from near-duplicate compounds appearing in both training and test sets.

The senior scientist's reflex: never trust a structure you have not looked at, and never trust a dataset you have not cleaned.

keyPoints: SMILES writes a molecule as text: atoms, = and # bonds, ( ) branches, digits for rings, lowercase for aromatic atoms.
Canonical SMILES is toolkit-specific; InChI is a standard, layered IUPAC identifier.
InChIKey is a 27-character hash of the InChI, ideal for searching but not reversible.
@/@@ encode tetrahedral stereo and / \ encode double-bond geometry in isomeric SMILES.
Key databases: PubChem, ChEMBL, DrugBank, ZINC, PDB; always standardize data before modelling.

Aspirin: acetyl ester and carboxylic acid on a benzene ring.
L-alanine, with its stereocentre encoded by @@.

test.q: Which database is best known for curated bioactivity data extracted from medicinal chemistry papers?

Only charged molecules have multiple SMILES

test.q: What symbols mark tetrahedral stereocentres in SMILES?
test.explain: @/@@ give tetrahedral configuration; / and \ give double-bond (E/Z) geometry.

test.q: In SMILES, CC(=O)O is ___ acid.

test.q: What 27-character hashed identifier is derived from a Standard InChI and used for web searches?
test.explain: The InChIKey is a fixed-length hash of the InChI, convenient for search engines and database lookups.

test.q: What is the name of the query language that extends SMILES for substructure searches?
test.explain: SMARTS lets you specify patterns such as 'any carboxylic acid'.

lessons.title: Molecular descriptors & fingerprints

levels.kid:
How do you describe a molecule with numbers? You could say how heavy it is, how greasy it is, and how many hooks it has for grabbing water. These numbers are called **descriptors**. They are like a molecule's height, weight and shoe size.

A **fingerprint** is a long row of light switches. Each switch is on if the molecule has a certain little piece, and off if it does not.

To see if two molecules are alike, a computer compares their switches. Lots of matching switches means they are probably cousins.

Chemists use these numbers to guess which molecules might make good medicines before they ever make them.
levels.hs:
A **molecular descriptor** is a number calculated from a structure that captures some property. Common ones in drug design:

- **Molecular weight (MW)**: size. Aspirin is about 180.
- **logP**: how much the molecule prefers fat-like solvent over water (lipophilicity). Higher = greasier.
- **Hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors**: counts of N–H/O–H groups and N/O atoms.
- **TPSA (topological polar surface area)**: the surface area of polar atoms, in Å². High TPSA means the molecule struggles to cross cell membranes.
- **Rotatable bonds**: a measure of flexibility.
- **Fsp3**: the fraction of carbons that are sp3 (non-flat). Ibuprofen's is about 0.46.

Rules of thumb combine descriptors. Lipinski's rule of five warns about poor oral absorption if a molecule has more than one of: MW over 500, logP over 5, more than 5 donors, more than 10 acceptors. Veber's rules suggest at most 10 rotatable bonds and TPSA at most 140 Å². Brain drugs usually need even lower TPSA.

A **fingerprint** turns a structure into a long string of 0s and 1s, each bit recording whether a particular fragment is present. Comparing fingerprints with the **Tanimoto coefficient** (shared bits ÷ total bits set in either) gives a similarity score from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical fingerprints). Chemists use this to find look-alike molecules in huge databases.
levels.college:
Descriptors range from simple counts to quantum-chemical quantities. Common classes:

- **Constitutional**: MW, heavy atom count, ring count, aromatic ring count, Fsp3.
- **Physicochemical**: calculated logP (e.g. Wildman–Crippen atom contributions, ClogP fragment methods), logD at pH 7.4 (which needs pKa), calculated pKa, molar refractivity.
- **Topological/polar**: TPSA (Ertl, 2000), computed by summing tabulated fragment contributions of N, O and attached hydrogens (optionally S and P), so no 3D structure is needed. Rough guides: TPSA up to about 140 Å² for oral absorption (Veber, 2002), and below about 90 Å², often much lower, for CNS penetration.
- **Efficiency metrics**: ligand efficiency LE ≈ 1.37 × pIC50 ÷ heavy atoms (kcal/mol per heavy atom), and lipophilic efficiency LipE (LLE) = pIC50 − logP (or logD). These reward potency gained without bloating size or lipophilicity.

**Fingerprints** encode structures as bit vectors.

- **Dictionary (key-based)**: each bit is a predefined substructure, e.g. the 166 public MACCS keys.
- **Path-based**: hash all linear paths up to a length (Daylight-type).
- **Circular**: ECFP/Morgan fingerprints (Rogers and Hahn, 2010) iteratively encode each atom's environment out to a radius; ECFP4 corresponds to radius 2 (diameter 4). They are hashed and folded to a fixed length such as 2048 bits, so unrelated fragments can collide on the same bit.

**Tanimoto similarity** T = c ÷ (a + b − c), where a and b are bits set in each molecule and c bits set in both. Its meaning depends on the fingerprint: a Daylight-fingerprint Tanimoto of 0.85 was historically used as a similarity threshold, whereas ECFP4 values are lower for the same pair. Aspirin and salicylic acid score only about 0.45 with ECFP4 because small molecules have few bits and one change alters many of them.

Descriptors and fingerprints feed QSAR models, virtual screening, diversity selection and property prediction.
levels.phd:
Descriptors are compressed views of a molecule, and the compression defines what a model can learn.

The **similar property principle** (molecules that look alike tend to act alike) underlies similarity searching and QSAR, but it fails at **activity cliffs**: pairs with high structural similarity and large potency differences, such as an added methyl that locks a conformation or a nitrogen that creates or breaks an H-bond. Matched molecular pair analysis quantifies typical effects of a single transformation across many series and exposes context dependence.

Fingerprint behaviour has statistical artefacts. Tanimoto similarity is biased by molecular size: small molecules set few bits, so single changes produce large drops in similarity, while large molecules saturate bits and look spuriously similar to one another. Folding introduces collisions. Count-based fingerprints and alternative metrics (Tversky for asymmetric queries, Dice) mitigate some of this. Score distributions for random pairs depend on the fingerprint, so thresholds must be calibrated against background distributions rather than transferred between methods.

Computed physicochemical descriptors carry substantial error. ClogP methods disagree by a log unit or more for complex molecules, especially ionizable, zwitterionic or intramolecularly H-bonded ones. TPSA ignores conformation, so intramolecular hydrogen bonds or chameleonic macrocycles that hide polarity in membranes (as proposed for cyclosporine) are poorly described; 3D polar surface area or experimental chromatographic measures help.

Modern machine learning has moved partly from handcrafted descriptors to learned representations: graph neural networks operating on molecular graphs, and transformer models on SMILES. These can outperform fingerprints on large datasets but are less interpretable and not always better on the small, noisy datasets typical of individual projects. Applicability domain matters in both cases: predictions for molecules far from the training set, measured by fingerprint distance, are unreliable.

Efficiency metrics have their own critiques. LE depends non-linearly on size and on the arbitrary standard state, prompting size-corrected variants; LipE is simpler and generally favoured for tracking optimization.
levels.expert:
On a team, descriptors are the dashboard and fingerprints are the search engine.

**Tracking optimization.** Experienced chemists plot potency against logD or heavy atom count for the whole series. Progress that comes only from adding lipophilicity ("molecular obesity") tends to bring solubility, metabolism, promiscuity and toxicity problems. Targets like LipE above about 5 for an optimized candidate and keeping logD in roughly the 1–3 range for oral drugs are common heuristics, though each target class has its own comfort zone.

**Property forecast indices.** Composite scores (such as GSK's property forecast index, which combines chromatographic logD with aromatic ring count, or the CNS multiparameter optimization score from Pfizer, which combines six properties including TPSA, pKa and HBD) help triage compounds. They are guides, not gates; many successful drugs break them, especially natural products, macrocycles and drugs that use transporters.

**CNS projects.** Teams aim for low TPSA, few hydrogen-bond donors (often 0–1, at most 2–3), moderate basicity and low P-glycoprotein efflux. A single extra amide N–H can turn a brain-penetrant compound into a peripheral one, which is also a deliberate strategy: second-generation antihistamines reduce sedation largely because they cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.

**Similarity searching in practice.** Use several fingerprints, look at the top hits by eye, and remember that a low Tanimoto does not mean dissimilar biology. For freedom-to-operate and patent work, chemists search by substructure (Markush) rather than similarity.

**Model skepticism.** Ask what data a property model was trained on, how far your molecule lies from it, and what the experimental assay variability is. A predicted solubility for a novel chemotype is a hypothesis; measure early.

**Pitfalls.** Calculated logP for zwitterions and strongly basic amines is often badly off; logD measurements are better. Descriptors computed on the wrong protonation state, a salt form left in the SMILES, or a missing stereocentre give silently wrong numbers.

The senior view: descriptors keep you honest about where potency is coming from.

keyPoints: Descriptors are numbers computed from structure: MW, logP/logD, HBD/HBA, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Fsp3.
Lipinski: flag if more than one of MW > 500, logP > 5, HBD > 5, HBA > 10; Veber: ≤10 rotatable bonds, TPSA ≤140 Å².
Fingerprints are bit strings of fragments (MACCS keys, ECFP/Morgan circular fingerprints).
Tanimoto = shared bits ÷ bits in either; thresholds depend on the fingerprint used.
Ligand efficiency and LipE (pIC50 − logP) reward potency gained without adding size or grease.

examples.tr: Small, moderately polar and comfortably within Lipinski and Veber limits.

examples.src: Aspirin vs salicylic acid, ECFP4 Tanimoto about 0.45
examples.tr: Closely related molecules can score low because small molecules set few bits.

lessons.title: 2D vs 3D representations

levels.kid:
When you draw a molecule on paper, it looks flat, like a stick-figure drawing. That is a **2D picture**. It shows which atoms are holding hands.

But real molecules are not flat! They are 3D, like a toy you can hold and turn around. Some parts stick up toward you, and some point away.

Chemists draw special wedges to show this. A solid wedge means "this part points at you." A dashed wedge means "this part points away."

The 3D shape really matters, because a medicine has to fit into its protein like a hand fits a glove. A left glove will not fit a right hand, even though both look the same when drawn flat!
levels.hs:
The structures you see in textbooks are mostly **2D skeletal formulas**: lines for bonds, with carbons at corners and line ends, and hydrogens on carbon left out. They show **connectivity**, which atoms are joined to which.

Molecules are really 3D. Chemists show depth in several ways:

- **Wedge and dash bonds**: a solid wedge points toward you, a hashed wedge points away. These show the configuration of stereocentres.
- **Newman projections**: looking straight down a bond to show staggered and eclipsed conformations.
- **Chair drawings**: for six-membered saturated rings like cyclohexane and piperidine, with axial and equatorial positions.
- **Fischer and Haworth projections**: used for sugars and amino acids.

Computers store 3D structures as **coordinates**: x, y and z for every atom. Viewing programs like PyMOL show molecules as sticks, balls or surfaces, and can show a drug sitting inside its protein.

Why does 3D matter? Proteins are 3D and chiral. Two mirror-image molecules (enantiomers) have identical 2D drawings without wedges but can act very differently in the body. Also, a molecule is flexible: single bonds rotate, so it can take many shapes, called **conformations**. The shape it adopts when bound to its target is called the **bioactive conformation**.
levels.college:
A **2D representation** encodes the molecular graph: atoms, bonds, charges and, optionally, stereo descriptors. It is sufficient for registration, substructure search, fingerprints and most descriptors. Stereochemistry in 2D is conveyed by wedge/hash bonds or by CIP labels (R/S, E/Z); a drawing without them is stereochemically undefined.

A **3D representation** adds Cartesian coordinates, typically from:

- **Experiment**: small-molecule X-ray crystallography (Cambridge Structural Database), protein–ligand crystal structures and cryo-EM (PDB), and NMR.
- **Computation**: conformer generators (e.g. RDKit's ETKDG, OpenEye OMEGA) build 3D geometries from 2D input using distance geometry or rule-based fragment libraries, followed by force-field minimization (MMFF94 and others).

A flexible molecule is an ensemble of **conformers**. Rotation about single bonds produces staggered (anti, gauche) and eclipsed forms; rings adopt chairs, boats or envelopes. The **bioactive conformation** is usually not the global energy minimum in vacuum; ligands commonly bind in conformations a few kcal/mol above their minimum, and large strain energies are a warning sign of a wrong pose or poor ligand design.

Preparing a molecule for 3D work requires decisions that 2D can ignore: the protonation state at the relevant pH, the dominant tautomer, the stereoisomer, and explicit hydrogens.

3D enables methods 2D cannot: **docking** (placing a ligand in a protein pocket and scoring it), **3D pharmacophore models** (spatial arrangements of H-bond donors, acceptors, charges and hydrophobes), **shape-based screening** (overlaying molecular volumes, e.g. ROCS), and physics-based free-energy calculations.

Visual conventions in 3D software: stick, ball-and-stick, space-filling (CPK) and surface models, often coloured by element (C grey or green, N blue, O red, S yellow) or by electrostatic potential.
levels.phd:
The 2D/3D distinction is really a question of which degrees of freedom a representation fixes.

A 2D graph fixes constitution and, with stereo flags, configuration. It deliberately ignores conformation, which is why graph-based methods are fast, deterministic and robust, but blind to effects such as intramolecular hydrogen bonds, atropisomerism, ring puckering and conformational preorganization. Atropisomers are a striking case: rotation about a hindered biaryl or aryl–amide bond can be slow enough to give separable stereoisomers that a 2D graph without axial-chirality notation cannot distinguish. LaPlante's classification by rotational barrier, from rapidly interconverting (class 1) to stable for years (class 3), has become a practical framework for drug discovery.

3D representations carry their own uncertainties. Conformer ensembles from distance geometry plus force fields reproduce crystallographic ligand conformations reasonably well for drug-like molecules, but coverage degrades for macrocycles and highly flexible ligands, which need enhanced sampling. Force-field torsional parameters are a known weak point; quantum mechanical torsion scans are used to correct key dihedrals.

Crystal structures are models fitted to electron density, not direct observations of atoms. Ligand geometry in protein complexes can be distorted by refinement with poor restraints, and at moderate resolution (around 2.5 Å or worse), ring flips, alternative conformations and even ligand identity may be ambiguous. Metrics such as real-space correlation coefficient and ligand strain help judge reliability. Waters, metal ions and protonation states are rarely observed directly but strongly affect modelling.

Shape and electrostatics underpin 3D similarity. Gaussian overlap methods quantify volume similarity; field-based approaches compare electrostatic and steric fields. These can identify scaffold hops invisible to 2D fingerprints, at the cost of conformer dependence.

Beyond static coordinates, molecular dynamics treats structures as time-dependent ensembles. Binding kinetics, cryptic pockets that open transiently and allosteric communication are properties of ensembles, not single structures, pushing the field toward 4D (time-resolved) representations.
levels.expert:
In project work, the 2D drawing is the language of the team and the 3D structure is the reason things happen.

**Always draw with stereochemistry.** Specify every stereocentre and state whether a compound is racemic, a single enantiomer of known absolute configuration, or of known relative configuration only. Many errors in papers and patents come from a missing or flipped wedge.

**Use crystal structures critically.** Before designing around a PDB pose, check resolution, look at the electron density around the ligand and nearby side chains, and look for alternative conformations and bound waters. Teams with crystallography in house aim for structures of the actual series, because a similar compound can bind in a flipped orientation.

**Know your conformational preferences.** Experienced chemists carry intuition about torsions: amides prefer trans; aryl amides with an ortho substituent twist out of plane; 2-methoxy and 2-fluoro groups set biaryl and aryl ether torsions; an N-methyl can switch an amide to cis. Reviewing the Cambridge Structural Database for a fragment's preferred torsions is a fast check on a proposed bioactive conformation. Rigidifying a molecule into its bioactive conformation (cyclization, an ortho substituent, a fused ring) can boost potency and selectivity, while a design that requires a strained conformation usually fails.

**Docking is a hypothesis generator.** Scores correlate poorly with affinity across chemotypes. Use docking to check whether an idea fits and makes key interactions, not to rank-order compounds by a number. Inspect poses by eye, check strain, and test predictions with a few cheap compounds.

**Atropisomers matter for development.** If a biaryl or hindered amide has a rotational barrier that allows slow interconversion, regulators expect it to be treated like a stereocentre: either fast enough to be one entity or stable enough to be developed as a single isomer. Sotorasib is an example of a drug developed as a single stable atropisomer.

The senior chemist's habit: look at every key compound in 3D in its pocket before making it.

keyPoints: 2D drawings show connectivity; wedges (toward viewer) and hashes (away) show configuration.
3D structures store x, y, z coordinates from experiment (X-ray, cryo-EM, NMR) or computation.
Flexible molecules exist as many conformers; the bioactive conformation is usually not the global minimum.
3D work needs protonation state, tautomer and stereoisomer decisions; it enables docking, pharmacophores and shape screening.
Crystal structures are models fitted to density; check resolution and ligand fit before trusting a pose.

examples.tr: Solid points toward the viewer, hashed points away; together they define R or S at a stereocentre.
A KRAS G12C inhibitor developed as a single, stable atropisomer.
